quote: We are descended from those who argued most persuasively that the good of the tribe meant executing their hated rival Uglak.
content: This is an evolutionary just-so story of exactly the kind the surrounding essays claim to teach readers to distrust. The ethnographic record of mobile foragers points the other way: such societies are aggressively egalitarian, and the people who get killed by coalitions are typically would-be dominators who bully or manipulate, not their victims (Boehm 2012). The nearest real theory, that human reasoning evolved for argumentation, predicts that people are also good at evaluating others' arguments, which is the opposite of a population pushed around by whoever talks best (Mercier & Sperber 2011). No data on ancestral executions exist; "we sure ain't descended from Uglak" is a rhetorical flourish standing in for evidence.

quote: you are guaranteed to be looking at an output that was optimized only for inclusive genetic fitness
content: There is no such guarantee. What you are looking at is the joint product of selection, drift, mutation bias, pleiotropy, developmental constraint, and historical contingency, and a large fraction of genomic and organismal features are not adaptations for anything (Lynch 2007; Gould & Lewontin 1979). Even where selection dominates, whether "inclusive fitness" is the quantity it maximises is disputed among theorists; a prominent 2010 attack on the framework drew a rebuttal signed by over a hundred biologists, and the dust has not settled (Nowak, Tarnita & Wilson 2010; Abbot et al. 2011). The essay needs a "pure note" to calibrate against, so it declares one to exist.

quote: What was the actual laboratory result? Cannibalism.
content: One laboratory result, chosen because it is ugly. Wade selected for small subpopulations and got beetles that ate each other's offspring; Muir selected hens on group productivity and got birds that stopped cannibalising each other, with mortality falling from 68% to 9% (Muir 1996). If the essay's method were applied honestly it would have to say that the "pure optimization for a known criterion" yields kindness or cruelty depending on the criterion, which is true but not the lesson being sold. Using a single cherry-picked outcome as the standard against which to judge human rationalisation is itself a fake optimisation criterion.

quote: you can just observe that people disagree about office politics in ways that strangely correlate to their own interests
content: The general phenomenon of motivated reasoning is real (Kunda 1990), but the specific claim that political positions track self-interest is one of the more surprising failures in political psychology. Decades of survey work find that narrow material self-interest is a weak predictor of policy attitudes; group identity, values, and symbolic politics predict far more (Sears & Funk 1991). People routinely and sincerely support policies that cost them money. The "just observe" is doing the work of a citation, and what one observes when one actually looks is not what the essay says.
